title: Recall Vote

jokes.text: Tom's fabricated story about Jaden Smith wanting to quit entertainment to work at Rent-a-Swag, and Tom nobly telling him the world needs him
jokes.setup: Tom is describing how well business is going at Rent-a-Swag
jokes.punchline: He invents a scenario where a celebrity wanted to abandon his career to work there, and Tom magnanimously turned him away for the good of humanity
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures Tom's delusional grandiosity — he can't just say business is good, he has to inflate it into a celebrity mythology where he's the magnanimous one. The choice of Jaden Smith specifically (a celebrity known for philosophical pronouncements) adds texture. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Jaden Smith wants to quit acting and work at Rent-a-Swag full-time. He says there's no better way to build a personal brand.

jokes.text: Tom responds to a serious buyout offer by announcing he needs 'a big old mug of hot chocolate, put on my thinking PJs, and get back to you'
jokes.setup: The lawyer has delivered a stern, time-pressured buyout offer and tells Tom to take it
jokes.punchline: Tom deflates the high-stakes business moment with cozy domestic self-care language
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The contrast between the tense business negotiation and 'thinking PJs' is sharp and specific. 'Thinking PJs' is a brilliantly specific made-up item that sounds exactly like something Tom would own and name. Highly quotable, tight structure, perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I need to go home, put on my thinking PJs, and make some hot chocolate before I can make a decision this big.

jokes.text: The lawyer expresses interest in acquiring Tom's 'thinking PJs' as part of the deal; Tom declares them and his 'YouTube blazer' nonnegotiable
jokes.setup: Tom introduced the 'thinking PJs' as a joke; now the lawyer plays it straight by including them in the offer
jokes.punchline: Tom has a 'YouTube blazer' too, and both items are deal-breakers — treated with total seriousness
jokes.explanation: The escalation here is excellent — the joke from #2 is immediately built upon. The lawyer's straight-faced interest in the PJs is funny, but the real punchline is Tom having a 'YouTube blazer' as a separately-named item. The deadpan delivery of 'nonnegotiable' treating a blazer-named-after-YouTube as a serious asset is top-tier Tom Haverford absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Those aren't just pajamas. Those are my thinking PJs. I do my best problem-solving in those things. You can't put a price on innovation.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And my snuggle sweatshirt? That's a legitimate business expense. It keeps me comfortable, which keeps me sharp, which makes me money. It's an investment in my future.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You're looking at this all wrong. These aren't ridiculous clothing items. These are tools. Valuable tools that have directly contributed to my success in business and in life.

jokes.text: Larry arrives late; when asked for his excuse, he says he was voting for Leslie. Leslie shuts down any recall talk.
jokes.setup: Leslie is exasperated that Larry is late to the meeting on the morning of her recall election
jokes.punchline: His entirely innocent and supportive excuse (voting for her) is met with the same brisk dismissal she'd give any bad excuse
jokes.explanation: A nice small character beat — Leslie's rigid suppression of recall anxiety causes her to steamroll even good news. Functional and character-consistent but not a standout.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Larry, you're late again. Do you have any idea how inconsiderate that is?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Actually, I was helping organize the surprise birthday party for you.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh... well, that's... I feel terrible now.

jokes.text: Someone at the haunted house meeting complains their assignment card says 'silly skeleton room' when it should say 'undead serial killer room'
jokes.setup: Leslie is giving out assignments for the City Hall haunted house
jokes.punchline: One person's correction is not a practical error but a tone/branding complaint — they want it scarier and more specific
jokes.explanation: A quick, functional background joke about civic over-investment in haunted house theming. The specificity of 'undead serial killer' vs 'silly skeleton' is amusing. Minor, but earns its beat.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm upgrading from 'silly skeleton' to 'undead serial killer' this year.

jokes.text: Leslie in confessional: 'Plus, um... It's Kevin Pollak's birthday. That's something to focus on today. Who cares about the recall? It's Kevin's day.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to convince herself she's fine on recall day by listing things she can focus on
jokes.punchline: She pivots to Kevin Pollak's birthday as a completely arbitrary celebrity non-event, delivered with forced conviction
jokes.explanation: Very well-constructed confessional joke. Leslie's coping mechanism of latching onto a random celebrity birthday as an emotional anchor is both funny and revealing of her anxiety. 'Who cares about the recall? It's Kevin's day' is a great line — the false equivalence is perfectly delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Did you know today is Dwayne Johnson's birthday? The Rock! Can you believe it? We should do something special. Maybe we could get the whole department together and make him a cake. A really big cake. With his face on it. In frosting. I think that would be a great use of our time right now.

jokes.text: Tom asks Ron to put more tiny marshmallows in his 'hot chocky'
jokes.setup: Tom is stressed about the business decision and sitting in Ron's office
jokes.punchline: The diminutive 'hot chocky' and the image of Ron Swanson — stoic, macho, man's man — serving Tom hot chocolate with tiny marshmallows
jokes.explanation: The visual of Ron Swanson as hot-chocolate-servant is inherently funny given his character. 'Hot chocky' is a perfect Tom diminutive. The contrast between Ron's stoicism and this domestic service role is strong character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, I'm stressed about this business deal. Can you help me relax?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Come on, just make me a hot chocky?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not making you a hot chocolate with baby talk, Tom. You're a grown man.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Please? With the little marshmallows?

jokes.text: Ron says 'Maybe you should try taking a walk... Out of my office'
jokes.setup: Ron appears to be offering genuine comfort to Tom, beginning a sensitive suggestion
jokes.punchline: The apparent advice is actually a dismissal — he finishes the sentence as an eviction
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection structure executed with economy. Sets up as genuine advice, pivots to dismissal. Very Ron Swanson — he pretends to soften but he doesn't. The pause implied before 'out of my office' is the key. High economy score because it achieves maximum effect with minimal words.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, I'm really going through something right now. I could use a friend.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm sorry to hear that. That sounds terrible. Anyway, I have a meeting.

jokes.text: Annabel Porter's bio: former face of the Eagleton phone book, moved to Hollywood to pursue her dream of 'becoming friends with a bunch of celebrities', then became a lifestyle guru. She's legit — she spent four months in Kate Bosworth's pool house.
jokes.setup: Ben explains to Ron who Annabel Porter is and why she's influential
jokes.punchline: Her credentials are hilariously insubstantial — phone book model, professional celebrity-friend, and the proof of her legitimacy is living in someone's pool house
jokes.explanation: Sharp satirical take on lifestyle influencer culture — the escalating absurdity of her 'credentials' lands well. 'She's legit' followed immediately by 'pool house' is a great structure. Eagleton phone book is a nice Pawnee universe detail.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, you're in this lifestyle magazine!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You're IN it! Ron Swanson, lifestyle icon!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't understand.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: They did a whole spread on you! 'Ron Swanson: America's Most Interesting Man!'

jokes.text: Annabel's Bloosh recommendations: Ron's chair, red quinoa, wind therapy, and buying an island — all presented as equivalent trends
jokes.setup: The group reads Annabel's Bloosh newsletter recommendations
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from vaguely trendy (quinoa) to pseudoscientific (wind therapy) to completely insane (buying an island) — all with the same casual lifestyle-guru confidence
jokes.explanation: The list-joke structure works well here — the escalation from quinoa to island-buying is a solid absurdist comedy beat. 'Wind therapy' is the funniest item because it exists in a real-seeming wellness space while being completely made up.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Annabel Porter is a lifestyle guru with an impressive resume. She's written three books, hosted a talk show, and most impressively... she's lived in someone's pool house.

jokes.text: Ben explains that buying an island is the only real way to ensure your goji-berry farm is pesticide-free
jokes.setup: The group is processing the list of Bloosh trends
jokes.punchline: Ben deadpans the logical underpinning of island-buying in terms of goji-berry pesticides, as if this is a completely reasonable explanation
jokes.explanation: A nice follow-through on the island joke, expanding its absurdity with faux-practical logic. Ben's deadpan delivery of this insane reasoning is where the comedy lives.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Annabel Porter's credentials are impeccable. She's got the work ethic, the drive, the ambition. Her only dream is friendship.

jokes.text: Tom announces a new leather jacket; Ron says he doesn't want one; Tom says 'It's for me. This is a great day!'
jokes.setup: Ron is listed in Bloosh; Tom announces someone is getting a leather jacket, implying it's for Ron
jokes.punchline: It was always for Tom — he was never thinking of Ron
jokes.explanation: Quick and clean. The beat of Ron shooting it down and Tom not even having intended it for him is a nice small misdirect. Short, well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Bloosh says the key to a healthy lifestyle is sustainable organic farming. So I'm buying an island.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm gonna grow my own vegetables, raise my own chickens, live off the land completely.

jokes.text: The whole office erupts in 'Ron's in Bloosh!' chant, including people who don't know what Bloosh is
jokes.setup: Tom excitedly announces Ron's Bloosh feature
jokes.punchline: The contagious chanting spreads to people who have no idea what Bloosh is, including Ron's confused 'What?'
jokes.explanation: The running repetition of the chant, capped by Ron's bewildered 'What?' and the instruction 'Do it', captures the Parks and Rec ensemble energy well. Infectious and charming.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, I got you a gift to celebrate your success.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't want your gift, Swanson.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, joke's on you because I was always planning to keep it for myself anyway.

jokes.text: Chris to April: 'April, you seem depressed, and I would know. I spent most of last year being treated by Dr. Richard Nygard for my own emotional problems.'
jokes.setup: Chris approaches April to help her
jokes.punchline: His attempt to establish empathy immediately pivots to a detailed disclosure about his own therapy — with the doctor's full name — which undercuts any comforting authority
jokes.explanation: Very Chris Traeger — the specific full name of the therapist and the overly earnest pivot to his own problems is perfect character comedy. Establishes his arc this season while landing as a joke.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: April, I can see you're going through something. I've been there. My therapist says I have a tendency to over-compartmentalize my emotions, which is ironic because I also over-share at inappropriate times. Last week I cried at a Cinnabon because it reminded me of my childhood, and the employee had to call her manager. But the point is, I'm here for you.

jokes.text: April reveals that every year she and Andy would 'dress up like demons and egg Larry's house', and Larry reacts with surprise ('That was you?')
jokes.setup: April is explaining Halloween traditions she had with Andy
jokes.punchline: The casual admission that they annually vandalized Larry's home — and his stunned recognition — is the punchline
jokes.explanation: Great ensemble beat. Andy and April egging Larry annually while dressed as demons is perfectly in-universe. Larry's genuine surprise ('That was you?') followed by April completely shutting him down ('Larry, please. We're having a private conversation') is a perfectly structured three-beat joke.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Every Halloween, Andy and I pick the most annoying person we know and we mess with them all day.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, we follow them around, we move their stuff, we tell them their fly is down when it's not...

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Wait. That was you two? On Halloween? Moving my things around?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, Larry. You're the most annoying person we know.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I want to file a complaint about this harassment.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You can file it with yourself. You're the Parks Department.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, you're the guy. You have to investigate yourself.

jokes.text: Chris attempts to cheer April up with 'scary, scary monster claws' — clearly a childish gesture
jokes.setup: Chris promises to make Halloween fun for April like Andy would
jokes.punchline: His attempt is 'scary, scary monster claws' — presumably him wiggling his fingers — a profoundly insufficient substitute for Andy
jokes.explanation: The inadequacy of Chris's attempt is the joke — he's sweet but completely wrong about what April needs. The gap between his confident declaration and the actual delivery lands as mild cringe comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Hey April, I'm going to try something Andy would do. Okay, here goes... RAWR! I'm a scary monster!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Chris, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Being playful and fun! Isn't this how Andy cheers people up? I'm not very good at this, am I?

jokes.text: The Leslie Knope Emotional Support Task Force has YouTube videos of turtles and birds becoming friends ready
jokes.setup: Ben explains what the task force has prepared for Leslie's recall day
jokes.punchline: 'YouTube videos of turtles and birds becoming friends' as a core emotional support tool, presented seriously alongside back rubs
jokes.explanation: Deeply specific and right for Leslie's character — YouTube videos of unlikely animal friendships is exactly the kind of wholesome content that would help Leslie. The specificity ('turtles and birds') elevates it above a generic 'cute videos' joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Larry, that jack-o-lantern looks like a blob. It's just a blob with a knife through it.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, my wife thinks it's great.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Your wife also thinks you're a good dancer.

jokes.text: The task force has a fake Lilith Fair concert poster — 'It's fake, but it'll buy us an hour'
jokes.setup: Ben is listing what the task force has prepared
jokes.punchline: Among legitimate comfort items is a fabricated concert poster for a defunct festival — and the calculated utility of it ('buy us an hour') is treated as standard procedure
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely great joke. Lilith Fair as a specific Leslie-appropriate cultural reference, combined with the matter-of-fact 'it's fake, but it'll buy us an hour,' shows deep character knowledge deployed with comic precision. It reveals how well her friends know her AND how willing they are to manage her. High quotability and rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Did anyone else notice that we missed the perfect opportunity to call it a 'Boo-reau of Land Management'? A BOO-reau? We had it right there and we didn't use it. That's fine. That's fine. I'm fine.

jokes.text: The task force's secret hand signal is 'loosely based on the Klingon greeting salute'; one member says if he'd known, he wouldn't have agreed to it
jokes.setup: Ben explains the task force's emergency signal system
jokes.punchline: The signal's Klingon basis is revealed as if it's a minor detail; a task force member retroactively objects
jokes.explanation: A decent geek-culture joke that also pokes at Ben's nerd tendencies. The retroactive objection is a nice small beat. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I made a fake concert poster of Radiohead coming to Pawnee. I'm going to put it up around town, and Leslie will see it and be so excited. Then, right before the concert date, I'll tell her it got cancelled. She'll be devastated for exactly four to six hours, and then I'll surprise her with actual Radiohead tickets I bought.

jokes.text: Ann suggests painting toenails like pumpkins as a distraction; Leslie calls her a 'genius' and says her brain is 'almost as perfect as your face'
jokes.setup: The task force is trying to distract Leslie from haunted house stress
jokes.punchline: Leslie's over-the-top compliment ('your brain is almost as perfect as your face') is another iteration of her constant veneration of Ann's beauty
jokes.explanation: A reliable running gag. Leslie's Ann compliments are always warmly funny, though by this point in the series they're a familiar note rather than a fresh joke. This one's a bit generic compared to more inventive iterations.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Okay, so we have this secret hand signal. You do this thing where you touch your nose and then point at someone.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: It means 'I got you.'

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's the signal from E.T.!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What? No, it's not.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yes it is! E.T. phone home. That's literally E.T.'s thing.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

jokes.text: Tom says 'Hey Ron, baby, what are the hot deets on Bloosh?' — Ron responds 'Start over and speak differently'
jokes.setup: Tom tries to excitedly ask Ron about the Bloosh PR situation
jokes.punchline: Ron refuses to engage with Tom's vocabulary and demands he speak like a human being
jokes.explanation: 'Start over and speak differently' is a perfect Ron Swanson line — maximum contempt, minimum words. The contrast between Tom's slang-dense enthusiasm and Ron's complete refusal to engage is a great dynamic. Highly economical.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I need to make sure every detail of this haunted house is perfect. The fog machine positioning, the jump scare timing, the actor rotations...

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Or we could all just do nail art and call it a day?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, no.

jokes.text: Tom and Donna's prepared cocktail banter for Ron: 'Annabel, could I be more jels of your low-lights right now?' and 'O.M.Squee, talk about bangs envy'
jokes.setup: Tom and Donna have written Ron a script of fashionable conversation snippets for the lifestyle event
jokes.punchline: The dialogue is so foreign to Ron's character that hearing him presumably read it is inherently absurd; 'O.M.Squee' as a portmanteau of OMG and squee is peak Tom invention
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. 'O.M.Squee' is an inspired piece of Tom-language invention. The specific crafting of this lifestyle jargon — low-lights, bangs envy — shows real writing effort. It's funny both as a lifestyle satire AND as character comedy (Tom/Donna's script vs. Ron's persona). 'Jels' as short for jealous is also perfect. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's a great idea, Ann. You're like the human version of a calculator. You have a brain, but no face.

jokes.text: After hearing the banter script, Ron says 'I regret everything'
jokes.setup: Ron has just heard the lifestyle banter he's expected to perform
jokes.punchline: 'I regret everything' — a sweeping existential statement applied to agreeing to attend this event
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum Ron Swanson. The leap from 'this banter is bad' to 'I regret everything' (his whole life, all choices) is a classic Ron overstatement delivered deadpan. Extremely economical. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yo, Ron, that meeting was straight fire, no cap. We were really popping off in there, you feel me?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have no idea what you just said. Please never speak again.

jokes.text: The news anchor announces the recall result before even asking 'too close to call?' — immediately: 'These are three phrases you won't hear tonight, as Leslie Knope has been voted out'
jokes.setup: The group settles in for a long night of election results; the anchor lists the usual close-race clichés
jokes.punchline: Before the audience expects the twist, the anchor reveals it was never close — the setup phrases are preemptively denied
jokes.explanation: Well-structured bit — the anchor begins with 'too close to call, a real nail-biter, anybody's game' then says those are three things you WON'T hear. The pivot is clean and the joke is in the structure itself. Not just a sad plot beat — it's written to be darkly funny.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay Ron, listen. In lifestyle magazines, we have our own language. You gotta learn to speak it if you want to be taken seriously.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: For example, we don't say 'muscles' anymore. We say 'jels.'

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's idiotic.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And we don't say 'Oh my God.' We say 'O.M.Squee.'

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not saying that.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And 'bangs envy' is when you see a woman with bangs and you want them.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why would anyone want bangs? They cover your face.

jokes.text: As everyone processes the devastating loss, Larry enters singing a pizza jingle ('I got-a the pizza, pizza time, it's-a pizza time!') with the pizzas he went to get
jokes.setup: Leslie has just been called as recalled; the room is devastated and silent
jokes.punchline: Larry arrives with pizzas, completely oblivious, singing an improvised pizza song
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The timing is perfect — the devastating result followed immediately by Larry's oblivious pizza jingle is a masterclass in tonal whiplash. The song itself ('I got-a the pizza, pizza time') is delightfully Larry-specific. Leslie's 'everyone is miserable and you are only making it worse' lands because the audience has experienced both beats. High craft for structural precision and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have no idea what any of these words mean. Lifestyle. Hashtag. Bitcoin. I don't understand any of it.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: That's because you're old.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not old. I'm... I'm just not interested in things.

jokes.text: Leslie's post-loss outgoing voicemail is described as 'sobbing and burping and crazy laughing'
jokes.setup: Ann reports on Leslie's emotional state after leaving her 30 voicemails
jokes.punchline: The voicemail description — sobbing, burping, and crazy laughing — captures a specific, visual emotional spiral
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'sobbing and burping and crazy laughing' as the voicemail's contents is very funny — burping is the unexpected middle element that makes the joke. The casual delivery while everyone waits anxiously adds to it.

dialogue.speaker: News anchor
dialogue.line: We're still waiting for the results to come in from several key precincts. It's far too early to call this race.

dialogue.speaker: News anchor
dialogue.line: The margin is razor-thin. Every vote will matter in this incredibly close election.

dialogue.speaker: News anchor
dialogue.line: Actually, we're getting word that the race is completely over. One candidate won by forty points.

jokes.text: Ben says Leslie is 'actually handling it pretty well' — immediately cut to Leslie walking in saying 'What's up, fartwads?'
jokes.setup: Ben reassures the group that Leslie is doing okay
jokes.punchline: Leslie enters calling everyone 'fartwads' — technically she IS doing okay by Leslie-post-crisis standards, which makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom juxtaposition — Ben's reassurance immediately undercut by Leslie's entrance. 'Fartwads' is a great Leslie-specific insult-that-isn't-really-an-insult. The joke works on two levels: the visual undercut AND the fact that she IS kind of fine.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Buongiorno! I brought-a the cannoli for the celebration! Why-a everybody look so sad?

jokes.text: Leslie eating a Paunch Burger after spending years boycotting it: 'Who cares now, right? What does it matter? Nothing matters anymore. Mmm. Oh, my God. This is good. This is really good. Why did I ever fight this?'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been a vocal opponent of Paunch Burger (junk food chain she's fought against for public health reasons)
jokes.punchline: Defeat unlocks the boycott and the burger is genuinely delicious — her nihilistic reasoning immediately gives way to real pleasure
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-based comedy. This works because it requires years of established character — Leslie's anti-junk food crusade — and then uses that history to make a simple burger transcendent. The shift from 'nothing matters' nihilism to genuine food ecstasy ('Oh, my God. This is good') is a great comedic arc compressed into four lines. High character integration and earned score.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: She left me this voicemail where she was just crying and hyperventilating. She said, 'Ann, I can't feel my face. Is my face still there? I think my face fell off.'

jokes.text: Leslie's drafted concession speech: 'Eat my shorts, Jabronies. Knope, out.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks if she's thought about a concession speech; she says she wrote one
jokes.punchline: The entire speech is the two-sentence wrestling-heel dismissal, read aloud with full seriousness
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top jokes. The contrast between what a concession speech should be (gracious, statesman-like) and what Leslie wrote in grief ('Eat my shorts, Jabronies. Knope, out.') is perfectly judged. 'Jabronies' is a wrestling insult that's somehow exactly right. 'Knope, out' as a mic-drop exit is inspired. The follow-up ('I thought it best to revisit at a later time') perfectly closes the beat. Extremely quotable and very high craft.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hey guys! What's up, buttheads?

jokes.text: Leslie, in defiant denial, insists the haunted house needs 'a papier-mâché li'l Sebastian'
jokes.setup: The group is trying to gently guide Leslie toward processing her loss and thinking about her concession speech
jokes.punchline: Leslie redirects to an absurdly specific haunted house addition — a papier-mâché li'l Sebastian — as a way to avoid her feelings
jokes.explanation: Li'l Sebastian is a beloved show mythology reference — a miniature horse treated as a deity by Pawnee. Leslie proposing a paper-mâché version for the haunted house as emotional avoidance is both character-true and funny. Strong for fans of the show.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've been working on my concession speech. I want it to be gracious and humble, you know?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Dear voters of Pawnee, you are all idiots. Congratulations on your terrible decision. I hope you enjoy your new terrible leader while I go to Harvard and become president, which I will definitely do. Signed, Leslie Knope, Future President and Current Smartest Person.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I'm gonna go fall asleep on a bench.'
jokes.setup: After processing the shock of the news with everyone, Ron announces his next move
jokes.punchline: His chosen response to the situation is to fall asleep on a bench — not go home, not offer comfort, just a bench
jokes.explanation: Pure Ron Swanson economy. No comment on the loss, no comfort offered — just a sleep announcement and a venue. The specificity of 'a bench' rather than at home is the twist. Very quotable, perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We could add Li'l Sebastian to the haunted house!

dialogue.speaker: Everyone
dialogue.line: *horrified silence*

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: *exits*

jokes.text: Joan Callamezzo introduces Annabel: 'I can honestly say today's guest is the only person in this town who's a bigger deal than I am'
jokes.setup: Joan is introducing Annabel Porter on her show Pawnee Today
jokes.punchline: Joan's introduction is simultaneously a compliment to Annabel and an assertion of her own importance — she can't introduce someone without ranking herself
jokes.explanation: Joan Callamezzo's narcissism is always well-deployed. Her inability to compliment someone without centering herself is character-specific and economically executed.

jokes.text: Joan says 'as a journalist, I feel like we're best friends' — immediately upon meeting Annabel
jokes.setup: Joan begins her interview with Annabel
jokes.punchline: Her claim to journalistic authority is immediately undermined by an unprofessional declaration of instant friendship — the opposite of journalism
jokes.explanation: A quick, clean Joan joke. The juxtaposition of 'as a journalist' with 'I feel like we're best friends' efficiently skewers her character.

dialogue.speaker: Annabel
dialogue.line: This sectional is absolutely delicious.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not going to eat furniture.

jokes.text: Annabel: 'The average woman worries about what she looks like in a bathing suit. So does my nanny. So I get it.'
jokes.setup: Annabel is performing relatable humility about not being perfect
jokes.punchline: Her version of 'getting it' is relating to her nanny — revealing the profound obliviousness of her supposed empathy
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke and one of the episode's best. The structure is perfect: 'I'm not perfect' > relatable concern about bathing suits > pivot to 'my nanny has that problem, so I get it.' The logic is airtight within her worldview while being completely tone-deaf. It efficiently establishes Annabel's character in one brilliant sentence. Very quotable and rewatch-worthy.

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: Where's the scary stuff?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Oh, well, the real scary stuff isn't in here. It's out there. It's student debt, it's choosing the wrong career, it's realizing your parents are just making it up as they go along, it's wondering if you're ever going to find someone who loves you, it's watching your metabolism slow down, it's wondering if you're going to die alone...

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: This is a fun house.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I know, buddy. I know.

jokes.text: Annabel's current trends: 'Mozambique cashmere is the new cast-iron stove'
jokes.setup: Annabel is listing her current lifestyle recommendations
jokes.punchline: The format '[X] is the new [Y]' applied to two completely unrelated luxury/utility items — Mozambique cashmere and cast-iron stove — creates nonsense lifestyle wisdom
jokes.explanation: Inspired piece of lifestyle parody. The '[X] is the new [Y]' formula is a real lifestyle media cliché, but applying it to Mozambique cashmere vs. cast-iron stove creates surreal nonsense that perfectly skewers the genre. Highly economical. One of the episode's sharper satirical lines.

dialogue.speaker: Kid
dialogue.line: Can I have some candy?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I have some bad news. You've already peaked. It's all downhill from here. So no candy for you.

jokes.text: Annabel mentions 'conflict-free paella recipes' and her fishmonger makes house calls ('Thank God. Finally.')
jokes.setup: Annabel continues listing her favorite things
jokes.punchline: Conflict-free paella as a category implies paella is usually morally compromised; Joan's 'Thank God. Finally.' treats a home-visiting fishmonger as a universal relief
jokes.explanation: 'Conflict-free paella' is a sharp satirical concept — applying ethical sourcing language to a casual dish. Joan's 'Thank God. Finally.' is a great reaction beat, playing her enthusiasm as shared universal relief.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay kids, I know today was scary, but remember - you're all very brave! And as the great poet Robert Frost once said, 'The woods are lovely, dark and deep, and I have miles to go before I sleep, and miles to go before I sleep.' So... don't lose hope!

jokes.text: Ron, backstage, asks: 'Did that woman call my chair delicious?'
jokes.setup: Annabel has just described Ron's chair as 'deliciously bold'
jokes.punchline: Ron's reaction isolates the word 'delicious' and is clearly offended/baffled by a food-adjacent adjective applied to his woodwork
jokes.explanation: Perfect Ron reaction beat. His precision with language — noting specifically that 'delicious' is the wrong word for furniture — is in character and lands cleanly. Maximum economy.

dialogue.speaker: Annabel
dialogue.line: You could use that chair as a throne, or a meditation seat, or even a lectern for important announcements!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's a chair. I sit in it.

jokes.text: Leslie answers the door in haunted house costume to kids and begins dispensing nihilistic Halloween wisdom: 'Scary stuff is invisible, Leah... Broken dreams, disappointment, achieving your greatest goal and having it all fall apart'
jokes.setup: Kids arrive at the City Hall haunted house expecting traditional scares
jokes.punchline: Leslie has pivoted the haunted house into an existential crisis confessional aimed at children
jokes.explanation: Outstanding character comedy. The scene of Leslie, still in costume, delivering true adult grief to trick-or-treaters who just want candy is deeply earned — it requires her entire character arc to land. 'Scary stuff is invisible, Leah' is a great opening line. This is the kind of joke that makes Parks and Rec special: it's emotionally true AND funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I went to this amazing new restaurant last night. It's called 'Deconstructed Essence of Potato.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That sounds pretentious.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: It was! They served me three peas on a slate tile for $47.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Three peas? I could get a whole bag of frozen peas at the grocery store for two dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: But these were artisanal peas, Jerry. They were hand-selected from a farm in Vermont.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Ann, that's insane. You paid $16 per pea.

jokes.text: Kids ask for candy; Leslie says 'I'm gonna give you something sweeter than candy, Ryan... The truth. It's very possible that some of you have already peaked.'
jokes.setup: Children at the haunted house ask for candy
jokes.punchline: Leslie offers 'the truth' and informs small children that they may have already peaked in life
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. 'Something sweeter than candy' as a setup with 'the truth' as the pivot is already good; the specific content of the truth — that these children may have already peaked — is shocking and perfect. Using children's first names ('Ryan') while telling them their best years may be behind them is cruelly specific. Deeply earned by Leslie's arc, structurally perfect, extremely quotable. This is what a 9 looks like.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: I need everyone to be quiet. I have an important announcement.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Your hair looks really nice today.

dialogue.speaker: Annabel
dialogue.line: Well, yes. I've been using a conditioning treatment derived from Icelandic glacier water and the tears of a endangered species.

jokes.text: 'It's all downhill from here, turkeys.' — Leslie to trick-or-treaters
jokes.setup: Leslie has told the kids they may have peaked
jokes.punchline: The follow-up dismissal 'turkeys' extends the nihilistic Halloween speech with a weirdly affectionate insult
jokes.explanation: 'Turkeys' as the dismissive closer for a motivational-speech-turned-nihilism is inspired. It's affectionate enough to be Leslie but devastating enough to land as a punchline. The brevity is perfect — 'it's all downhill from here' then one word.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm going to scare April. I'm going to hide behind this corner and jump out.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Wait, why can I see myself in this mirror? April's going to see me coming from a mile away.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: There are mirrors everywhere in this hallway. How is anyone supposed to scare anyone in a government building?

jokes.text: Leslie corrects the departing teacher: 'It IS Ms. Knope. It's not city councilwoman Knope, because that chapter of my life is already over.'
jokes.setup: A teacher tries to hustle the kids away and says 'say goodbye to Ms. Knope'
jokes.punchline: Leslie insists on the correction with total seriousness — the title precision becoming its own joke about her identity crisis
jokes.explanation: A nice follow-through on the Halloween nihilism sequence. The fact that she's still formally correcting the teacher while in full meltdown mode is funny and character-true.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm going to channel Andy's energy and just be super positive and enthusiastic about everything.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's not going to work. You're being weird.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: What? I'm being authentic. This is who Andy is.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, you look like an FBI agent trying to go undercover at a Rascal Flatts concert.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Well, that's oddly specific, but I think the FBI would actually be less believable in that scenario.

jokes.text: 'Just remember, kids. Nothing gold can stay.'
jokes.setup: Leslie closes her Halloween encounter with the children
jokes.punchline: Closing with a Robert Frost quote delivered as Halloween wisdom to children visiting a haunted house
jokes.explanation: A fitting end to the children's haunted house sequence. Frost's 'Nothing Gold Can Stay' as Leslie's closing statement is unexpectedly literary and perfectly timed. The image of this line being delivered to Halloween trick-or-treaters by a grieving politician is tragicomically Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: The problem is that you're trying too hard. You're like, aggressively optimistic. It's exhausting. I can't even mock you properly because you just absorb it and turn it into something positive. It's infuriating.

jokes.text: Joan introduces herself to the Pawnee Today audience as 'America's greatest leader'
jokes.setup: Joan returns from commercial break to continue the interview
jokes.punchline: She describes herself as 'America's greatest leader' — not journalist, not host, but leader
jokes.explanation: Consistent Joan narcissism — 'America's greatest leader' is a funny escalation of her self-regard. Functional character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm failing as both a boyfriend and a government employee. That's... that's two things. Two distinct things that I'm failing at.

jokes.text: Annabel says chairs can be used 'as a focal point in your yoga tent'; Ron responds 'Put it by a table and eat a meal'
jokes.setup: Annabel is giving elaborate lifestyle suggestions for Ron's chairs
jokes.punchline: Ron's flat, practical alternative ('put it by a table and eat a meal') undercuts all the pretension with pure common sense
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ron line. The yoga tent vs. 'put it by a table and eat a meal' contrast is a perfect distillation of Ron's character — chairs are for sitting at tables, food is for eating. His utter refusal to engage with lifestyle language is quintessential. Very high economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Look, I know how you feel. When I was mayor of Ice Town, I got impeached. It was a really dark time for me.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: But I got through it, and you will too.

jokes.text: Annabel says she doesn't do 'meals' — every two hours she has a 'food tease' like an 'oat wedge' or 'seaweed lozenge'
jokes.setup: Ron has suggested using a chair to eat a meal
jokes.punchline: Annabel corrects the concept of meals entirely — she has 'food teases' every two hours, including an 'oat wedge' and 'seaweed lozenge'
jokes.explanation: 'Food tease' as a lifestyle food concept is inspired. 'Oat wedge' and 'seaweed lozenge' are meticulously crafted fake foods — they sound exactly like real wellness foods while being ridiculous. High originality for inventing these specific terms.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, I was on the Student Government in high school. I was President.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's great!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, it's not. I think that might have been the peak of my life.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What are you talking about? You're the Deputy City Manager.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, but I was *President* in high school. That's a bigger title.

jokes.text: Annabel, mid-interview, interrupts to compliment Joan's hair: 'I think this is really important, so I need everyone to shut up... I love your hair.'
jokes.setup: The interview is proceeding; Annabel begins a statement suggesting something crucial
jokes.punchline: The urgent subject — requiring everyone to shut up — turns out to be a hair compliment
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed misdirect. The escalating importance of 'I need everyone to shut up' creates expectation, then the subject is trivial. Also works because Joan visibly loves it, which reveals her vanity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, Ben, look at this lamp! It's so... cylindrical! Why is it cylindrical?! That's genius!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. This couch. This couch is just fabric stretched over wood. WHO THOUGHT OF THAT? That person deserves a medal!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The floor is so... flat! It's like a big, flat rectangle that goes all the way across!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This window is basically just a hole that lets you see outside! That's INSANE!

jokes.text: Joan on her hair: 'It's genetic and unattainable.'
jokes.setup: Annabel compliments Joan's hair
jokes.punchline: Joan's response isn't 'thank you' or false modesty — it's a clinical assessment that simultaneously brags and dismisses the compliment
jokes.explanation: Four words, perfect joke. 'Genetic and unattainable' as a hair compliment response is a masterpiece of character economy — it's arrogant, dismissive, and almost scientific, all at once. The 'unattainable' element implies she's already considered whether others could replicate it and determined they cannot. Extremely quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, when we get in there, let me do the talking. I've prepared some talking points.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, you don't need talking points. Just be yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's the problem, Ron. I need you to tell her that I'm very successful, that I have many leather-bound books, and that my apartment smells of rich mahogany.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Those are all things I say about myself.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I know. And it works for you.

jokes.text: Chris attempts to scare April in the haunted house mirror maze — April immediately says 'I can see you. There's like a million mirrors in front of me.'
jokes.setup: Chris in a monster costume tries to sneak up on April
jokes.punchline: His attempt fails immediately and obviously — the very mirrors meant to create atmosphere made him completely visible
jokes.explanation: A functional physical comedy beat — the mirror maze backfiring is obvious but executed well. April's flat 'there's like a million mirrors' is a nice deadpan response.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I believe in craftsmanship. If you're going to make something, make it right. Use quality materials, take your time, and put care into every detail.

dialogue.speaker: Annabel
dialogue.line: That's nice, Ron. You know, the Chinese make things really cheap and fast. We should probably just buy everything from them.

jokes.text: Chris as 'Bert Macklin, friendly lifeguard'; April corrects: 'Bert Macklin is not a lifeguard. He's an FBI agent.' Chris: 'Really? That's even harder to believe.'
jokes.setup: Chris tries another character to cheer April up — Andy's alter ego Bert Macklin, but reimagined as a 'friendly lifeguard'
jokes.punchline: April corrects the lore; Chris accepts the correction and then observes that the FBI agent version is even more unbelievable
jokes.explanation: The Andy mythology callback works well. The twist is Chris's logical response — he accepts the FBI correction and then notes that's somehow even less believable than his version. April's lore-precision and Chris's innocent agreement make this a strong character comedy beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I need to get back to my office.

dialogue.speaker: Annabel
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Where do you think you're going, you magnificent bastard? Get back here and tell me more about your woodworking!

jokes.text: Chris: 'I've failed you, both as a scary monster and a friend.'
jokes.setup: April tells Chris his attempts aren't working and she's doubly sad
jokes.punchline: Chris accepts failure in both categories simultaneously — 'scary monster' and 'friend' treated as equally serious roles he has not fulfilled
jokes.explanation: Great line. The parallel construction of failing as both a 'scary monster' and a 'friend' is funny because it treats the costume role with complete earnestness equal to the real friendship. Chris's sincerity makes it land. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I would like to make an official announcement. Ben and I are no longer intoxicated. We are completely sober. From this moment forward, we pledge to maintain the highest standards of sobriety and decorum.

jokes.text: Ben has been impeached: 'I was impeached when I was 18, and it was brutal.'
jokes.setup: Leslie says she feels like she's accepted her peak; Ben tries to relate
jokes.punchline: His point of empathy is being impeached at 18 — a callback to Ben's Ice Town backstory, delivered casually as relatable advice
jokes.explanation: A great payoff for longtime viewers. Ben's Ice Town shame being reframed as wisdom for Leslie's situation — and delivered with complete sincerity — is both funny and touching. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Pawn Shop Owner
dialogue.line: Yeah, sure, I can do that.

jokes.text: 'Oh, God, did I peak when I was 18?' — Ben, realizing he may have talked himself into believing his best years are behind him
jokes.setup: Ben tries to counter Leslie's nihilism by telling his Ice Town story as a comeback tale
jokes.punchline: Retelling it out loud, he realizes it might actually support Leslie's 'you've peaked' theory — his 18-year-old self ran a town
jokes.explanation: Excellent payoff. Ben's use of his own story as a cautionary tale backfires — the audience sees the irony before he does, and then he arrives at it too. 'Oh, God, did I peak when I was 18?' is a great line, and Leslie and Ann's immediate pivot to shots caps it perfectly. Great structure.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm thinking something really subtle. Maybe a small tattoo of the town seal, but with little fireworks coming out of it, and then the words 'Pawnee Forever' in a really cool gothic font, and then maybe some eagles, and a banner that says 'Leslie Knope Was Here,' and then the entire Bill of Rights in tiny letters around the edges, and then a hologram of me shaking hands with all the presidents, and then...

jokes.text: The shots are labeled 'B-13' and called 'Bird bath salts'; the venue/setting is clearly not a bar — then someone says 'Champagne decanters!'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ann are doing shots
jokes.punchline: The increasingly improvised nature of their drinking situation — mystery shots called 'bird bath salts', followed by the absurd luxury of 'champagne decanters'
jokes.explanation: The absurdist post-Bloosh-event drinking scene has some nice chaos energy. 'Bird bath salts' is a funny invented shot name; the random escalation to champagne decanters suggests the scene is gloriously uncontrolled.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Do you have anything for pain?

dialogue.speaker: Pawnshop Owner
dialogue.line: Yeah, I got this bucket of pills. I don't know what they are, but they're free.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not really a solution.

dialogue.speaker: Pawnshop Owner
dialogue.line: It's a bucket of solutions.

jokes.text: Lifestyle devotee tells Ron she needs 12 chairs for her stepdaughter's craft room; Ron says 'I make two a year, so maybe in six years'
jokes.setup: A wealthy Bloosh devotee wants to buy Ron's chairs in bulk
jokes.punchline: Ron's production rate makes the math on the request absurd — six years to fill the order — delivered without apology
jokes.explanation: Perfect Ron moment. His complete indifference to the business opportunity — just stating the math flatly — is quintessential character comedy. Extremely economical.

dialogue.speaker: Tattoo Artist
dialogue.line: So you want a tattoo of a compass pointing to your heart?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, a compass pointing to my *home*.

dialogue.speaker: Tattoo Artist
dialogue.line: Right, that's what I said. A compass pointing to your heart.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Ben, that's not what he said at all.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: This is going to be a problem, isn't it?

jokes.text: Another Bloosh devotee says she can't buy chairs if they were ever touched by someone who ate refined sugar, and she's protesting the event
jokes.setup: Various wealthy guests are competing to buy Ron's chairs
jokes.punchline: The refined-sugar contamination caveat is delivered as an utterly reasonable condition — and she's also protesting the entire event on this basis
jokes.explanation: A good one-off absurdist gag about wellness culture extremism. The refined-sugar furniture contamination theory and the instant protest escalation is funny, though the character is not developed enough to get full marks.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, listen to me. Tattoos are a sign that you haven't peaked. Think about it. The most successful people in the world? No tattoos. They peaked early, got comfortable, didn't need to mark their body to feel alive.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But us? We get tattoos because we're still climbing. We're still hungry. We're saying to the world, 'I am not done yet.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So actually, Ann, by getting a tattoo, we're guaranteeing that we will never peak.

jokes.text: Annabel wants to mass-produce Ron's chairs; Ron declines; Annabel: 'Yes, and now they will be made by thousands of tiny Chinese hands'
jokes.setup: Ron says mass-produced chairs wouldn't be Swanson chairs; Annabel agrees and pivots to outsourcing
jokes.punchline: Annabel's re-pitch completely contradicts any artisanal credibility she might have claimed — she's fine with overseas mass production
jokes.explanation: A sharp hypocrisy joke — the lifestyle guru championing handmade artisan goods immediately defaults to mass offshore production. The phrasing 'thousands of tiny Chinese hands' is Annabel's oblivious attempt at charm, which makes it land as character comedy rather than just a joke about manufacturing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, well, we'll see you later, Chief.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, take care, Ace.

dialogue.speaker: Pawnshop Owner
dialogue.line: My name is Gary.

jokes.text: Ron introduces Tom to Annabel: 'He's a big fan of your... Whatever you call what you do.' Then: 'Please speak to each other while I leave.'
jokes.setup: Ron wants to escape Annabel's pitch; he introduces Tom as a buffer
jokes.punchline: 'Whatever you call what you do' — Ron refusing to acknowledge lifestyle guruism as a real thing — followed by the explicit self-removal
jokes.explanation: 'Whatever you call what you do' is a great Ron line — deliberate ignorance as dismissal. The efficient 'Please speak to each other while I leave' is a perfect exit. Two strong lines back to back.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have a name. It's Ron. I like my name. It's short, it's simple, it's direct. When I die, I want people to remember my name. Not because I did anything special, but because it was a good name. That's all a person can hope for.

jokes.text: Ron introduces Tom to Annabel: 'This is my very good friend Tom Haverford. He's a big fan of your... whatever you call what you do.' Then: 'Please speak to each other while I leave.'
jokes.setup: Ron is using Tom as an escape hatch from Annabel
jokes.punchline: 'Whatever you call what you do' perfectly dismisses Annabel's entire career, and 'Please speak to each other while I leave' is Ron at his most formal and magnificent
jokes.explanation: 'Please speak to each other while I leave' is a nearly perfect Ron Swanson exit line. It's formal, polite, and utterly dismissive — he's essentially giving permission to have a conversation he's departing from. 'Whatever you call what you do' as a dismissal of a lifestyle guru is also excellent. This line is deeply character-integrated (only Ron) and highly quotable. Strong candidate for the episode's best Ron moment.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: When I die, I want my gravestone to be a solid gold statue of me, riding a solid gold motorcycle, doing a wheelie. And under it, it just says 'Tom Haverford: He Stayed Lit.' In Comic Sans.

jokes.text: Annabel: 'I am not done with you, you wicked little so-and-so.' Ron: 'Terrific.'
jokes.setup: Ron tries to escape the conversation
jokes.punchline: Annabel's flirtatious/aggressive 'wicked little so-and-so' is met with Ron's flat 'Terrific' — maximum sarcasm, minimum engagement
jokes.explanation: Ron's single-word 'Terrific' as a response to 'wicked little so-and-so' is perfectly Ron — the least engaged possible response. The dynamic between Annabel's flamboyance and Ron's flatness is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I was supposed to stop you from getting tattoos. But honestly, I find your complete disregard for consequences and your destructive ideas kind of... endearing.

jokes.text: Leslie and Ben in a pawnshop declaring they are 'sober' and want tattoos; the shop owner says it's a pawnshop but 'yeah, sure, I can do that'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben have decided to get tattoos to prove their love
jokes.punchline: They're at a pawnshop, not a tattoo parlor — but the owner has a side business in tattoos, normalized as completely ordinary
jokes.explanation: The meta-absurdity of a pawnshop tattoo artist who barely blinks at the request is a nice Pawnee-world building joke. Their insistence they're sober is also funny because it's clearly relevant context.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have to face facts. Ann is gone. She moved away. And I'm never going to see her again.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I mean, I'll see her again. But not like, all the time.

jokes.text: Leslie announces her plan to get tattoos: 'Hello, sir. We are sober. We would like to get tattoos on our bodies, 'cause we love each other.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has declared they need to 'do something big' to prove they haven't peaked
jokes.punchline: Her opening line to the tattoo artist ('We are sober') is the most unconvincing possible sobriety claim — announcing it unprompted immediately signals the opposite
jokes.explanation: A great gag. 'We are sober' as a voluntary opening statement is perfect — it's exactly what a drunk person who knows they shouldn't be doing this would say. Leslie's earnest overexplaining ('because we love each other') adds to the comedy. The pawnshop setting (for a tattoo parlor) also lands as a background visual gag.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're like a poetic and noble land mermaid.

jokes.text: Leslie's tattoo idea: a portrait of Eleanor Roosevelt with a tattoo of Pat Benatar on HER arm — then 'No, scratch that. Just write Ben.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is designing her tattoo
jokes.punchline: She elaborates an increasingly complex meta-tattoo concept (a tattooed tattoo within a portrait) before abandoning all of it for the simplest possible option
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The escalating specificity of the Eleanor Roosevelt tattoo concept — not just Eleanor, but Eleanor with a Pat Benatar tattoo on her arm — is absurdist genius that also fits Leslie's character perfectly (feminist icon meets rock icon). Then the complete collapse to 'just write Ben' is a perfect anticlimax. Very Leslie, highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm being weird because I miss Andy. It's temporary weakness. Once he gets back, I'll return to normal and stop saying things like 'I love you' and 'I'm glad you exist.'

jokes.text: The pawnshop owner asks 'Okay, you said you wanted mouth queen?'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben's tattoo session has been proceeding
jokes.punchline: The owner has apparently noted down 'mouth queen' as Leslie's requested tattoo text — she immediately shuts everything down
jokes.explanation: A great punchline to the pawnshop sequence — 'mouth queen' appears out of nowhere as the tattoo that was apparently requested (presumably by drunk Ben or Leslie offscreen) and the contrast with 'just write Ben' is hilarious. Leslie's immediate 'stop it, stop everything that you're doing' is a perfect response.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're in love with me.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm not in love with you. I'm in love with Ann.

jokes.text: Ann arrives at the pawnshop and Leslie says 'Ann! Ann wants a tattoo!' while Ann protests
jokes.setup: Ann arrives to save Leslie and Ben from the tattoo
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately attempts to recruit Ann into the tattoo scheme she was just about to be talked out of
jokes.explanation: A nice small beat — Leslie pivoting from being about to leave to immediately trying to pull Ann in. Shows drunk Leslie's escalation instincts.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm selling out. And I'm not ashamed about it. Selling out is what successful people do. It's the American dream.

jokes.text: Pawnshop owner: 'Okay, you said you wanted mouth queen?' Leslie: 'No, stop. Stop it. Stop everything that you're doing.'
jokes.setup: The tattoo process is underway at the pawnshop
jokes.punchline: 'Mouth queen' as what the tattoo artist understood Leslie to have requested — the horror of a near-miss
jokes.explanation: 'Mouth queen' is a perfectly terrible tattoo — it's specific enough to be funny and just ambiguous enough to be alarming. Leslie's immediate 'stop everything' is the right reaction. Good dark-subversive gag about the dangers of drunk decision-making in a pawnshop.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie's like a toddler after a nap. She just wakes up and is ready to take on the world again.

jokes.text: Ben insists what they're doing is not nuts: 'We are merely getting tattoos so that everybody knows we love each other and that we haven't peaked.'
jokes.setup: Ann is trying to talk them out of the tattoos
jokes.punchline: 'Merely getting tattoos' as a minimizing opener for a plan that still includes 'we haven't peaked' as a motivating reason is self-aware about how nuts it sounds while still defending it
jokes.explanation: Ben's drunk-logical defense of the tattoos is funny because he's clearly the logical one and yet 'we haven't peaked' remains in the justification. The word 'merely' doing heavy lifting in front of 'getting tattoos' is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And this one is Ben as a sexy pumpkin.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No surprise.

jokes.text: Ann: 'So say goodbye to the nice man and thank me for saving you from being on Dateline.'
jokes.setup: Ann is extracting Leslie and Ben from the pawnshop
jokes.punchline: The implicit narrative of the situation — drunk couple gets pawnshop tattoos — is coded as a Dateline NBC segment, reframing the whole event as a cautionary true-crime story
jokes.explanation: A sharp, funny line. The Dateline reference recontextualizes the whole scene as a cautionary-tale narrative, which is an earned observation. Ann's straight-man energy is well-used here.

jokes.text: Leslie and Ben say goodbye to the pawnshop owner: 'Good-bye, world traveler.' 'Later, bro Heisen.'
jokes.setup: Ann is forcing them out; they say goodbye to the pawnshop owner
jokes.punchline: Two entirely different unprompted nicknames for the same man — 'world traveler' (Leslie) and 'bro Heisen' (Ben) — with no explanation
jokes.explanation: Drunk character goodbye nicknames — 'bro Heisen' especially is a funny invented nickname that sounds like something Ben Wyatt would say when drunk. 'World traveler' for a pawnshop owner is also a nice absurd choice.

jokes.text: Tom tells Ron there's no shame in failure; Ron points out people want to give Tom money. Tom says Ron didn't sell his chairs 'because you value your name.' Ron says his gravestone will be important. Tom: 'My gravestone's gonna be a 60-inch touchscreen with a hologram of four mes singing End of the Road by Boyz II Men... But point taken.'
jokes.setup: Ron is giving Tom a speech about the value of one's name; Tom appears to receive the wisdom
jokes.punchline: Tom's conception of a gravestone — a 60-inch touchscreen with a hologram of four Toms singing a Boyz II Men song — is so elaborately Tom that it earns its own category. Then he concedes the point anyway.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The specificity is extraordinary: not a touchscreen but a 60-inch touchscreen; not one Tom but four; not just any song but End of the Road by Boyz II Men (which is specifically about death/farewell and therefore grimly apt). Then 'but point taken' — he accepts Ron's wisdom while describing a grave marker that proves he has none. High originality, exceptional character integration. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: First rule of the Leslie Knope emotional support task force: 'Don't let her get a tattoo.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks Ben what the first rule of the task force is
jokes.punchline: The first rule — implying this is the most fundamental concern — is specifically about tattoos, suggesting they have dealt with this before
jokes.explanation: A great callback payoff. The task force was established earlier, and now we learn the most important rule — which also confirms they have needed to prevent Leslie tattoos before. The brevity and specificity of it is excellent.

jokes.text: Ben: 'I couldn't help it. She's so cute when she's coming up with destructive ideas.' Ann: 'Never send a husband to do a best friend's job.'
jokes.setup: Ben failed the task force's primary rule; Ann calls him out
jokes.punchline: Ann's line — a riff on 'never send a boy to do a man's job' — reframes the husband/best friend dynamic as a professional hierarchy in which Ann outranks Ben
jokes.explanation: Ann's line is sharp and quotable — the 'husband vs. best friend' professional hierarchy is funny and true to the show's relationships. Ben's excuse is also a good character line.

jokes.text: Ann catches Leslie avoiding her problems and confronts her; Leslie denies it and immediately asks 'Can we talk about this tomorrow?'
jokes.setup: Ann says Leslie is avoiding her problems
jokes.punchline: Leslie denies avoiding her problems and in the same breath asks to avoid the conversation until tomorrow
jokes.explanation: A well-timed self-own — the punchline is how quickly her denial gives way to the exact behavior she's denying. Classic sitcom irony but executed crisply.

jokes.text: 'Oh, it's so hard to read when you're drunk.'
jokes.setup: Ann has Leslie read her own crisis notes aloud
jokes.punchline: Leslie struggles and then identifies why — she's drunk — with complete matter-of-fact self-awareness
jokes.explanation: A good small beat in the emotional pivot scene. 'It's so hard to read when you're drunk' is an unexpected self-aware line that gets the audience chuckling during an otherwise sincere moment.

jokes.text: Ann: 'Ann, you poetic and noble land mermaid, you're right once again.' — Leslie calling Ann a 'poetic and noble land mermaid'
jokes.setup: Leslie is thanking Ann for helping her process the loss
jokes.punchline: 'Poetic and noble land mermaid' as a Leslie-style compliment — the running gag of her elaborate Ann compliments reaches an especially lush iteration
jokes.explanation: 'Poetic and noble land mermaid' is one of the best Leslie-Ann compliments in the series. The unexpected 'land mermaid' as an archetype, modified by 'poetic and noble', is genuinely inventive. This is among the most quotable lines in the episode and the type of specific absurd compliment that made Parks and Rec famous. Extremely high quotability.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I flushed my car keys down the toilet.' Ann: 'No problem.'
jokes.setup: The emotional scene has resolved; Leslie is wrapping up
jokes.punchline: As a throwaway coda, Leslie casually reveals she flushed her car keys — Ann's 'No problem' accepts this as a manageable situation
jokes.explanation: Excellent comedic coda to the emotional scene. 'I flushed my car keys down the toilet' delivered casually after a sincere moment is perfectly timed. Ann's unflappable 'No problem' shows she's accustomed to this level of Leslie chaos. The unexpectedness and economy make this a strong joke.

jokes.text: April apologizes to Chris: 'I'm sorry I said you were lame, okay? You are, but I know you were just trying to help me, so... Thank you.'
jokes.setup: April approaches Chris to apologize for dismissing his help
jokes.punchline: The apology includes a reaffirmation of the insult — 'you are [lame]' — making it a non-apology apology that's perfectly in April's voice
jokes.explanation: Classic April delivery — the kindness buried inside something that sounds like an insult. The pause implied before 'you are' (confirming the lameness) while still expressing genuine gratitude is April in a nutshell. High character integration.

jokes.text: Chris: 'And if you want to egg Larry's house, come find me.'
jokes.setup: Chris and April have reconciled
jokes.punchline: Chris offers to continue the tradition of egging Larry's house as a bonding activity — despite being the HR-adjacent earnest wellness guy
jokes.explanation: Good callback. Chris offering to join the Larry egging tradition is funny because it's such an un-Chris activity. The callback to April's Andy tradition gives it warmth — he's trying to fill that role for her.

jokes.text: April: 'Also, if Chris puts that much effort into making my stupid night better, I'm sure that he'll make your lame life perfect. Or he's secretly super in love with me. It's probably that.'
jokes.setup: April is talking to Ann about Chris
jokes.punchline: She gives Ann a genuine recommendation then immediately pivots to claiming Chris is in love with her — with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: April's self-assurance that Chris is secretly in love with her is a nice piece of vanity-comedy from an otherwise self-deprecating character. The pivot from genuine sweetness to 'it's probably that' is characterful.

jokes.text: Chris, overhearing, corrects April: 'That's a funny joke, April. But the truth is, I'm very much in love with Ann.' April: 'Okay, gross. The spell's broken.'
jokes.setup: April has claimed Chris is secretly in love with her; Chris overhears
jokes.punchline: Chris's sincere correction (he loves Ann) followed by April's 'the spell's broken' — the nice moment she was having is immediately ruined by genuine human warmth
jokes.explanation: 'The spell's broken' is a perfect April Ludgate line — the brief emotional openness immediately closed by her persona. The timing of Chris's oblivious but sincere correction is good. Well-executed scene ender.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Ron said there's nothing more valuable than my name, but he's not a businessman. I am. And now I have seed money for my next venture. I sold out, baby.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just closed the deal by surrendering his name for extra money
jokes.punchline: He explicitly refutes Ron's wisdom — acknowledging he heard and understood it — and then announces 'I sold out, baby' with total self-satisfaction
jokes.explanation: 'I sold out, baby' as a proud declaration is very Tom — he's not ashamed, he's triumphant. His explicit rejection of Ron's wisdom while crediting it is great character work. The joy in his declaration makes it land.

jokes.text: Confessional: 'The thing about being part of the Leslie Knope emotional support task force is that it's a very easy job. She's never down for that long. And now that she's had a little time to recharge, she is like a toddler bouncing back from a nap.'
jokes.setup: Ben describes the task force in a confessional
jokes.punchline: 'Like a toddler bouncing back from a nap' — a perfectly specific simile for Leslie's resilience that's simultaneously affectionate and diminutive
jokes.explanation: 'Toddler bouncing back from a nap' is a great, specific image. It captures Leslie's energy, her brief emotional crashes, and her rapid recovery all in one economical comparison. Ben's knowing affection in the line makes it warm rather than cruel.

jokes.text: Leslie, re-energized, immediately launches at Ben: re-zoning, deck painting, color samples — and then reveals she's carved their faces into jack-o-lanterns, including 'Ben, you make a sexy pumpkin — no surprise'
jokes.setup: Ben has just described Leslie as bouncing back like a toddler after a nap
jokes.punchline: The immediate demonstration of her recovery — rapid-fire to-do items AND carved pumpkin faces, with the commentary 'you make a sexy pumpkin — no surprise'
jokes.explanation: Excellent payoff to Ben's confessional — the juxtaposition is immediate and complete. 'You make a sexy pumpkin — no surprise' is a lovely Leslie compliment to her husband. The speed and specificity of her recovery list is a great visual joke that confirms Ben's assessment.

tmdb_overview: Leslie tries to complete some of her biggest city council goals, like hosting an NFL Play 60 event with the Indianapolis Colts, and trying to add fluoride to Pawnee's drinking water. Meanwhile, Chris and Ron attempt to bond while building cribs for their future children.
insight: Recall vote chaos fuels 66 jokes across 43 minutes—character comedy peaks with cringe undertones.
